arXiv:2510.13748v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2025

Asymptotically optimal reinforcement learning in Block Markov Decision Processes

Thomas van Vuren Affiliation: Eindhoven University of Technology, The Netherlands    Fiona Sloothaak Affiliation: Eindhoven University of Technology, The Netherlands    Maarten G. Wolf Affiliation: Koninklijke KPN N.V., The Netherlands    Jaron Sanders Affiliation: Eindhoven University of Technology, The Netherlands
Abstract

The curse of dimensionality renders Reinforcement Learning (RL) impractical in many real-world settings with exponentially large state and action spaces. Yet, many environments exhibit exploitable structure that can accelerate learning. To formalize this idea, we study RL in Block Markov Decision Processes (BMDPs). BMDPs model problems with large observation spaces, but where transition dynamics are fully determined by latent states. Recent advances in clustering methods have enabled the efficient recovery of this latent structure. However, a regret analysis that exploits these techniques to determine their impact on learning performance remained open. We are now addressing this gap by providing a regret analysis that explicitly leverages clustering, demonstrating that accurate latent state estimation can indeed effectively speed up learning.

Concretely, this paper analyzes a two-phase RL algorithm for BMDPs that first learns the latent structure through random exploration and then switches to an optimism-guided strategy adapted to the uncovered structure. This algorithm achieves a regret that is O⁡(T+n)O(\sqrt{T}+n) on a large class of BMDPs susceptible to clustering. Here, TT denotes the number of time steps, nn is the cardinality of the observation space, and the Landau notation O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) holds up to constants and polylogarithmic factors. This improves the best prior bound, O⁡(T+n2)O(\sqrt{T}+n^{2}), especially when nn is large. Moreover, we prove that no algorithm can achieve lower regret uniformly on this same class of BMDPs. This establishes that, on this class, the algorithm achieves asymptotic optimality.

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

The field of machine learning, and artificial intelligence more generally, has taken society by storm. One of its key techniques, Reinforcement Learning (RL) [38], is applied everywhere. It is, for example, applied to problems in finance, games, healthcare, industrial control, and robotics.

However, despite its promise, RL still faces numerous practical challenges. One key difficulty is the curse of dimensionality [38], which can make learning in problems with large state spaces intractable. This challenge is particularly nasty because the state space size is often exponential in the number of system components.

These issues can be unavoidable if no additional structure is present in a system. There namely exist Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with nn states on which the expected regret after TT time steps is at least Ω⁡(n​T)\Omega(\sqrt{nT}) [34]. When nn is exponentially large, such regret can render RL impractical.

Fortunately, many real-world environments exhibit exploitable structure. For instance, if different states share similar transition probabilities, then we could first learn a clustering of the state space. This reduces the effective size of the state space, mitigating the impact of the curse of dimensionality.

1.2 State-space reduction in Block MDPs

In this paper, we conduct a regret analysis for an episodic learning strategy that exploits a state-space reduction technique tailored to Block Markov Decision Processes (BMDPs).

BMDPs [29] are MDPs in which observations are drawn from a large set of contexts. The transitions dynamics, however, are determined fully by just a few unobserved latent states. Specifically, each context xx is associated to a latent state s=f⁡(x)s=f(x), and the system moves from latent state ss to latent state s′s^{\prime} according to a transition kernel p⁡(s′∣s,a)p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a). The agent then observes only a context y∈f−1​(s′)y\in f^{-1}(s^{\prime}) drawn from the emission distribution q(⋅∣s′)q(\cdot\mid s^{\prime}). The map ff is called the latent state decoding function, and the presumed challenge is that it is hidden from the agent.

The structural assumptions just discussed are what make BMDPs interesting and different from generic MDPs. The remaining parameters, including the reward and episode structure, are summarized in Figure 1. Please see Section 2 for details.

Recently, a clustering technique developed for Block Markov Chains (BMCs) [35], inspired by techniques for (labeled) Stochastic Block Models (SBMs) [1, 45], was generalized to BMDPs [24]. Specifically, [24] mathematically studies a technique that estimates the latent state decoding function efficiently based on data generated under a fixed policy. This technique was then used in [24] to study the sample complexity of a reward-free RL algorithm. A regret analysis when exploiting these techniques, however, remained open. This gap is addressed in this manuscript.

In typical regret analyses, one studies not only specific algorithms that minimize regret but also the least amount of regret that every algorithm will acquire [8]. The fact that some regret will always be accumulated is, ultimately, because exploration must be balanced with exploitation.

Most methods tackle this so-called exploration–exploitation trade-off using the optimism–in–the–face–of–uncertainty principle [38]. It is implemented in MDPs by computing Upper Confidence Bounds (UCBs) on the estimated long-term reward following a visit to a state–action pair [6, 10, 46]. UCBs are added to the immediate reward during policy updates as an exploration bonus, encouraging visits to state–action pairs with uncertain value. This reduces uncertainty, leading to smaller bonuses and less exploration overall.

Now, in BMDPs, we can leverage the block structure by aggregating related transitions to reduce the value estimates’ variances. This yields tighter UCBs and smaller exploration bonuses, ultimately reducing regret. But, the quality of those value estimates would then depend on how well the block structure is estimated. Misclassified contexts induce biases and therefore complicate efficient exploration.

To avoid this source of approximation error, we adopt a two–phase approach by building on [24]. Under their structural assumptions, clustering techniques efficiently recover the latent structure through random exploration. This enables a sharp regret analysis, which we present in this paper.

1.3 Summary of results

1.3.1 Structural properties

We analyze the following subclasses of BMDPs:

Definition 1.1 (η\eta-Reachability).

Let η>1\eta>1 be independent of nn. A BMDP Φ\Phi is η\eta-reachable if it has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    maxa⁡maxs1,s2,s3​{p⁡(s2∣s1,a)/p⁡(s3∣s1,a),p⁡(s1∣s2,a)/p⁡(s1∣s3,a)}≤η\max_{a}\max_{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}\{p(s_{2}\mid s_{1},a)/p(s_{3}\mid s_{1},a),p(s_{1}\mid s_{2},a)/p(s_{1}\mid s_{3},a)\}\leq\eta;

  2. (ii)

    maxs⁡maxx,y∈f−1​(s)⁡q⁡(x∣s)/q⁡(y∣s)≤η\max_{s}\max_{x,y\in f^{-1}(s)}q(x\mid s)/q(y\mid s)\leq\eta; and

  3. (iii)

    for all sufficiently large nn, maxs1,s2⁡|f−1​(s1)|/|f−1​(s2)|≤η\max_{s_{1},s_{2}}|f^{-1}(s_{1})|/|f^{-1}(s_{2})|\leq\eta .

Definition 1.2 (ℐ\mathcal{I}-Identifiability).

Let ℐ>0\mathcal{I}>0 be independent of nn. An η\eta-reachable BMDP Φ\Phi is ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable if, for all sufficiently large nn, minx⁡Iη​(x,Φ)≥ℐ\min_{x}I_{\eta}(x;\Phi)\allowbreak\geq\allowbreak\mathcal{I}; see (15) for IηI_{\eta}’s definition.

A brief explanation of Definitions 1.1 and 1.2 is as follows. The reachability property ensures that random exploration achieves coverage of the observation space. The identifiability property ensures that it is information-theoretically possible to detect the latent states. The parameter IηI_{\eta} can be interpreted as a measure of separation between latent states. For more detailed discussion on Definitions 1.1 and 1.2, we refer to Appendix B.

1.3.2 Regret lower bound

Our first result is a regret lower bound for η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable BMDPs. To state it, let nn denote the number of contexts, SS the number of latent states, AA the number of actions, HH the episode horizon, KK the number of episodes, and TK=K​HT_{K}=KH the total number of time steps. We denote by RegK​(ℒ,Φ)\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi) the expected regret after KK episodes of a learning algorithm ℒ\mathcal{L} on the BMDP Φ\Phi; see (10) for the precise definition.

Theorem 1.3.

Assume that the following hold:

S=o(n),S/4∈ℕ≥2,H≥2,andA≥S/2.S=o(n),\quad S/4\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2},\quad H\geq 2,\quad\textnormal{and}\quad A\geq S/2. (1)

There exists a constant 𝔡>0\mathfrak{d}>0 independent of nn such that the following holds: for any η>1\eta>1 independent of nn and any learning algorithm ℒ\mathcal{L}, there exists a BMDP Φ\Phi with initial context distribution μ=Unif⁡([n])\mu=\mathrm{Unif}([n]) that is η\eta-reachable and Iη:=𝔡​η−1​(η−1)2/(η+1)3I_{\eta}:=\mathfrak{d}\eta^{-1}(\eta-1)^{2}/(\eta+1)^{3}-identifiable. If moreover TK=Ω⁡(n∨A)T_{K}=\Omega(n\vee A), then

RegK​(ℒ,Φ)=Ω⁡(A​TK+n).\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)=\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}+n). (2)

Theorem 1.3 identifies the two asymptotically leading regret contributions. Firstly, the Ω⁡(A​TK)\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}) term captures the cost of learning the latent state transition probabilities. Secondly, the Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) term encapsulates the cost of learning the latent structure.

1.3.3 Two-phase algorithm and regret upper bound

Our second result establishes that an explicit two–phase algorithm achieves near-optimal worst-case regret in η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable BMDPs. Algorithms 1, 3 and 2 in Section 4 contain the pseudocode.

The first phase consists of exploration happening uniformly at random. Its duration is set by a threshold Θclust\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}. Based on the observations made, the latent structure is estimated using [24, Algorithms 1 and 2]. The second phase uses an optimism–based strategy to balance exploration with exploitation while refining its transition probability estimates. It adapts [6, Algorithms 1 and 2], designed for MDPs without latent structure, by incorporating improved value estimates and smaller exploration bonuses that take advantage of the learned structure.

Theorem 1.4.

Assume that TK=Ω⁡(H4​S3​A)T_{K}=\Omega(H^{4}S^{3}A), A=nO⁡(1)A=n^{O(1)}, and S​H=O⁡(n)SH=O(n). Assume, moreover, that the BMDP Φ\Phi is η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable, and that μ=Unif⁡([n])\mu=\mathrm{Unif}([n]). If Algorithm 1 is run with threshold Θclust=ω⁡(n​A​(S3∨ln⁡n))\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}=\omega(nA(S^{3}\vee\ln n)), then for any c>0c>0,

RegK​(ℒ,Φ)=O~​(H​S​A​TK+n​S​H3+TK/nc+Θclust).\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)=\tilde{O}\bigl(H\sqrt{SAT_{K}}+nSH^{3}+T_{K}/n^{c}+\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}\bigr). (3)

Here, the notation O~​(⋅)\tilde{O}(\cdot) suppresses polylogarithmic factors.

To facilitate comparison with Theorem 1.3, consider that (3) implies for Θclust=n​S3​A​ln2​n\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}=nS^{3}A\ln^{2}n and TK=nO⁡(1)T_{K}=n^{O(1)} that

RegK​(ℒ,Φ)=O~​(H​S​A​TK+n⁡(S3​A+S​H3)).\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)=\tilde{O}\bigl(H\sqrt{SAT_{K}}+n(S^{3}A+SH^{3})\bigr). (4)

This result is optimal in the sense that it matches Theorem 1.3’s dependence on nn and TKT_{K} up to polylogarithmic factors.

It is also instructive to compare Theorem 1.3 to other regret bounds for BMDPs when clustering. The one paper closest in spirit that we found is [7]. There, the authors prove a regret bound for an online algorithm that also uses spectral methods. When specialized to η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable BMDPs, their bound is only O~​(D​S​A​T+n2​S​A)\tilde{O}(DS\sqrt{AT}\allowbreak+\allowbreak n^{2}SA). Here, DD bounds the time required to move between two contexts, replacing HH in their nonepisodic setting. Their result, however, does apply also to other BMDPs, not just η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable ones.

Our result improves the regret’s dependence on the number of contexts from O~​(n2)\tilde{O}(n^{2}) to O~​(n)\tilde{O}(n), at the cost of a greater dependence on SS, AA, and HH. This leads to a better bound for sufficiently large observation spaces, specifically when n=ω⁡(S2+H3/A)n=\omega(S^{2}+H^{3}/A). We achieve this by performing dedicated exploration, and incorporating the efficient latent state estimation algorithm from [24].

In addition, (4) improves the leading-order regret for large TKT_{K} by S\sqrt{S}. This is significant because [7] assumes rewards depend solely on the latent state. In this case it is unnecessary to learn the emission kernel, simplifying the analysis considerably. Our improvement stems from leveraging the algorithms and proof techniques in [6], rather than the earlier [23], upon which [7] builds.

1.4 Summary of proof techniques

1.4.1 Proof of the regret lower bound

Theorem 1.3’s proof is presented in Section 3. We define a class of hard–to–learn BMDPs, adapted from [24], and show that it includes instances inducing Ω⁡(A​TK+n)\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}+n) regret.

To establish the Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) contribution, we prove a new lower bound on the worst-case number of misclassifications of any latent state estimator on BMDPs in our class (see Proposition 3.13). Existing lower bounds, such as [24, Theorem 1] and the closely related [35, Theorem 1], do bound the number of misclassifications on any given BMDP, but only for algorithms satisfying a consistency condition. Instead, our class is such that any algorithm violating this condition must perform poorly on at least one instance. The construction is based on a construction used for random graph clustering [47].

The proof for the Ω⁡(A​TK)\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}) contribution leverages techniques developed for tabular MDPs [11, 36] These were in turn adapted from the literature on bandit learning [8]. A direct application of [11]’s construction to the induced MDP on the latent states would lead to an Ω⁡(H​S​A​TK)\Omega(\sqrt{HSAT_{K}}) lower bound for general BMDPs. However, the resulting instances would not be η\eta-reachable or ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable. We therefore modify those constructions to comply with Definitions 1.1 and 1.2. This leads to a slightly weaker but still Ω⁡(TK)\Omega(\sqrt{T_{K}})-type regret.

1.4.2 Proof of the regret upper bound

Theorem 1.4’s proof is presented in Section 5. We establish there that our algorithm’s first phase successfully recovers the latent structure. We subsequently bound the regret incurred during the algorithm’s second phase.

For the first phase, we refine [24]’s analysis of [24, Algorithms 1 and 2] in two ways. First, whereas [24] establishes exact latent state recovery with high probability as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, we provide an explicit probability bound. This is required for bounding the expected regret. Second, we relax their assumptions, allowing SS, AA and pp to depend on nn. Moreover, Definition 1.2’s condition is slightly weaker than its analogue in [24]; see Appendix B for a comparison. These relaxations are necessary, because we could only prove Theorem 1.3 under these weaker assumptions.

For the second phase, we leverage that Algorithm 1 has already recovered the latent structure exactly. In this case, the exploration bonuses need not account for uncertainty about this structure. This allows us to broadly follow the analysis of [6]. The main new difficulty arises from the structure of the BMDP kernel, involving both a latent state transition kernel and emission probabilities. Their estimators are statistically dependent, and a key part of our analysis is a decomposition that disentangles their contributions to the regret.

1.5 Related literature

Our work connects to the following three research directions.

1.5.1 Function approximation for block and low-rank MDPs

RL in BMDPs often uses function approximation. This assumes that the decoding- or value function belongs to a known, well-behaved function class ℱ\mathcal{F}. Prior work has used function approximation for Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning [29, 26, 9, 12, 49], which bounds the time required to find a near-optimal policy; reward-free learning [49, 31], where the agent explores without observing rewards; and regret minimization [14], which is the focus of this paper. These methods have also been applied to more general models such as low-rank MDPs [3, 42, 32, 30], which include BMDPs as special cases.

The use of function approximation is typically motivated by settings with infinite or continuous context spaces. Function approximation is then necessary to generalize to unseen contexts. By contrast, we consider BMDPs with finite context spaces and arbitrary decoding functions. In this case, [24] notes that function approximation achieves the same sample complexity scaling in nn as tabular methods. In other words, these methods do not exploit the inherent block structure, but instead benefit from the restrictions imposed by the class ℱ\mathcal{F}. We therefore also do not rely on function approximation or oracles for latent state estimation.

1.5.2 Latent state estimation and clustering in block models

Another line of research develops explicit algorithms for learning the latent structure from observations. This includes [7], which estimates the latent structure using a spectral method based on [4]. However, as explained in Section 1.3.3, this leads to suboptimal regret in the worst case. Instead, we build on [24], whose algorithm uses a two-step approach: an initial spectral estimate is refined using a likelihood-based improvement step. This approach was inspired by similar techniques developed for BMCs [35] (but see also [13, 48, 50, 43]), which, in turn, build on techniques for SBMs [44, 45].

[24] also shows that their algorithm is nearly optimal by deriving an information-theoretic lower bound. This is done using change-of-measure arguments, likewise inspired by [35, 44, 45]. As detailed in Section 1.3, our work adds to these developments in latent state estimation by proving a new lower bound on the number of misclassifications, and refining [24]’s analysis of their algorithm.

1.5.3 Regret minimization in MDPs with known structure

Recall that, after learning the latent structure, we adapt the optimism-based approach of [6] to minimize the regret while refining our transition probability estimates. We use specialized kernel estimates and bonus terms that exploit the latent structure, leading to improved regret. This approach has also been successfully applied to other types of structured MDPs. For instance, [40] designs exploration bonuses for factored MDPs, [17] for Markovian bandits, and [28] for linear MDPs. Similar two–phase approaches have also been considered in the context of bandit learning [18, 19, 25].

Linear MDPs in particular include BMDPs (with known latent structure) as a special case. One can therefore also use algorithms designed for linear MDPs after the initial structure-learning phase. However, because linear MDPs are more general than BMDPs, these algorithms do not fully exploit the discrete structure of BMDPs. They therefore do not achieve optimal regret on BMDPs, with the best regret bounds being O~​(S​A​H​TK)\tilde{O}(SA\sqrt{HT_{K}}) [20, 2, 22]. We exploit the additional structure of BMDPs to improve this by a factor of S​A\sqrt{SA} in Theorem 1.4.

2 Model definitions

Elementary notation

For m∈ℕ+m\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, let [m]:={1,2,…,m}[m]\vcentcolon=\{1,2,\ldots,m\}. Functions like v:[m]→ℝv:[m]\rightarrow\mathbb{R} are identified with vectors in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, with components v⁡(x)v(x) for x∈[m]x\in[m] relative to the standard basis. For v,w∈ℝmv,w\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, let ⟨v,w⟩\langle v,w\rangle denote the standard inner product. Finally, let Unif⁡(𝒳)\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{X}) refer to the uniform distribution on 𝒳⊂[m]\mathcal{X}\subset[m].

2.1 Block Markov Decision Processes

BMDPs are described by tuples Φ=(n,S,A,H,f,p,q,μ,r)\Phi=(n,S,A,H,\allowbreak f,\allowbreak p,\allowbreak q,\mu,r). Here, n,S,A,H∈ℕ+n,S,A,H\in\mathbb{N}_{+} denote the number of contexts, latent states, actions, and episode horizon, respectively. Unique to a Block MDP is that there is a decoding function f:[n]→[S]f:[n]\rightarrow[S] that assigns contexts to latent states, and that the latent states determine the dynamics. Specifically, BMDPs have a latent state transition kernel p:[S]×[A]×[S]→[0,1]p:[S]\times[A]\times[S]\rightarrow[0,1] and an emission kernel q:[S]×[n]→[0,1]q:[S]\times[n]\rightarrow[0,1]. Here, p⁡(s′∣s,a)p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a) is the probability of transitioning to state s′s^{\prime} given that the system is in state ss when choosing action aa, and q⁡(x∣s)q(x\mid s) the probability of observing context xx given that the system is in latent state ss.

The triple (f,p,q)(f,p,q) specifies the MDP’s transition kernel P:[n]×[A]×[n]→[0,1]P:[n]\times[A]\times[n]\rightarrow[0,1] completely. Specifically,

P⁡(y∣x,a):=p⁡(f⁡(y)∣f⁡(x),a)​q​(y∣f⁡(y))P(y\mid x,a)\vcentcolon=p(f(y)\mid f(x),a)q(y\mid f(y)) (5)

is the probability of transitioning to context yy given that the current context is xx when choosing action aa. Note that the probability of moving to context yy depends only on the current latent state and not the specific context.

Finally, r={rh}h∈[H]r=\{r_{h}\}_{h\in[H]} with rh:[n]×[A]→[0,1]r_{h}:[n]\times[A]\rightarrow[0,1] denotes a bounded, nonstationary and deterministic reward function that may depend on the context that is observed.

2.2 Policies

A memoryless policy π\pi is a collection π={πh}h∈[H]\pi=\{\pi_{h}\}_{h\in[H]} of mappings πh:[n]×[A]→[0,1]\pi_{h}:[n]\times[A]\rightarrow[0,1] where πh​(a∣x)\pi_{h}(a\mid x) denotes the probability of selecting action aa when observing context xx at round hh. Memoryless policies do not depend on the sequence of contexts prior to the current context. Because we may only consider memoryless policies, we will simply refer to them as policies.

Together, a BMDP Φ\Phi and a policy π\pi define a probability measure ℙΦ,π\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\pi} and a random variable (x1,a1,…,xH,aH,xH+1)(x_{1},a_{1},\ldots,x_{H},a_{H},x_{H+1}) representing the sequence of contexts and actions satisfying ℙΦ,π[x1=x]=μ(x)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\pi}[x_{1}=x]=\mu(x), ℙΦ,π​[ah=a∣xh=x]=πh​(a∣x)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\pi}[a_{h}=a\mid x_{h}=x]=\pi_{h}(a\mid x) and ℙΦ,π[xh+1=y∣xh=x,ah=a]=P(y∣x,a)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\pi}[x_{h+1}=y\mid x_{h}=x,a_{h}=a]=P(y\mid x,a).

Namely, starting from the initial condition VH+1π∗=0V_{H+1}^{\pi^{*}}=0, we can obtain an optimal policy and value function at round h∈[H]h\in[H] by setting

2.4 Episodic learning algorithms and regret

An episodic learning algorithm selects a policy for each episode based on its previous observations and the known reward function. Formally, such an algorithm is a collection ℒ={ℒk}k∈ℕ+\mathcal{L}=\{\mathcal{L}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}} of maps where for any Dk∈(([n]×[A])H×[n])k−1D_{k}\in(([n]\times[A])^{H}\times[n])^{k-1} and reward function rr, ℒk​(Dk,r)\mathcal{L}_{k}(D_{k},r) is a policy.

A BMDP and learning algorithm give rise to a probability measure ℙΦ,ℒ\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}} along with a sequence of random variables 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} for k≥2k\geq 2 representing the contexts and actions during the first k−1k-1 episodes:

𝒟k:=⊗k′=1k−1𝒟(k′)where𝒟(k′):=(xk′,1,ak′,1,…,xk′,H,ak′,H,xk′,H+1).\mathcal{D}_{k}\vcentcolon=\otimes_{k^{\prime}=1}^{k-1}\mathcal{D}_{(k^{\prime})}\quad\mathrm{where}\quad\mathcal{D}_{(k^{\prime})}\vcentcolon=(x_{k^{\prime},1},a_{k^{\prime},1},\ldots,x_{k^{\prime},H},a_{k^{\prime},H},x_{k^{\prime},H+1}). (9)

Then ℙΦ,ℒ[xk,1=x]=μ(x)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}[x_{k,1}=x]=\mu(x), ℙΦ,ℒ[ak,h=a∣xh=x,𝒟k]=πk,h(a∣x)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}[a_{k,h}=a\mid x_{h}=x,\mathcal{D}_{k}]=\pi_{k,h}(a\mid x), and ℙΦ,ℒ[xk,h+1=y∣xk,h=x,ak,h=a]=P(y∣x,a)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}[x_{k,h+1}=y\mid x_{k,h}=x,a_{k,h}=a]=P(y\mid x,a), where πk=ℒk​(𝒟k,r)\pi_{k}=\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{k},r) denotes the policy selected by ℒ\mathcal{L} for episode kk.

We define the regret of a learning algorithm ℒ\mathcal{L} on a BMDP Φ\Phi after KK episodes by

RegK​(ℒ,Φ):=∑k=1K𝔼Φ,ℒ​[V1π∗​(xk,1)−V1πk​(xk,1)].\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)\vcentcolon=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}\bigl[V_{1}^{\pi^{*}}(x_{k,1})-V_{1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,1})\bigr]. (10)

2.5 Latent state estimation

We also consider algorithms that estimate the latent structure based on a sequence of transitions of the BMDP. Formally, these are defined as a collection of maps 𝒞={𝒞k}k∈ℕ+\mathcal{C}=\{\mathcal{C}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}} where 𝒞k​(Dk,r)\mathcal{C}_{k}(D_{k},r) is a decoding function for any Dk∈ℋk−1D_{k}\in\mathcal{H}^{k-1} and reward function rr.

Given an estimated decoding function f^\hat{f}, we define the set of misclassified contexts in 𝒮⊂[S]\mathcal{S}\subset[S] as

ℰ(f^;f,𝒮):=∪s∈𝒮(f^−1(γ^f∗(s))∖f−1(s))withγ^f∗∈arg​minγ∈Perm⁡(𝒮)|∪s∈𝒮(f^−1(γ(s))∖f−1(s))|.\mathcal{E}(\hat{f};f,\mathcal{S})\vcentcolon=\cup_{s\in\mathcal{S}}(\hat{f}^{-1}(\hat{\gamma}^{*}_{f}(s))\setminus f^{-1}(s))\quad\mathrm{with}\quad\hat{\gamma}^{*}_{f}\in\argmin_{\gamma\in\mathrm{Perm}(\mathcal{S})}|\cup_{s\in\mathcal{S}}(\hat{f}^{-1}(\gamma(s))\setminus f^{-1}(s))|. (11)

For convenience, we also introduce the shorthand notation ℰ⁡(f^,f):=ℰ⁡(f^,f,[S])\mathcal{E}(\hat{f};f)\vcentcolon=\mathcal{E}(\hat{f};f,[S]).

We next recall an information-theoretic quantity from [24]. It controls the optimal misclassification count of certain well-behaved estimation algorithms; see [24, Theorem 1]. It is analogous to similar quantities controlling the optimal rate of cluster recovery in BMCs [35] and SBMs [47, 45].

Let Φ\Phi have decoding function ff, and define for any π\pi, ss, and aa,

Using the representation in [24, Eqn. (35)], the information-theoretic quantity is now given by

px,s~,c,ωin​(i,s,a):={ω⁡(s,a)​p​(s~∣s,a)​c​q​(x∣f⁡(x)),if ​i=1,ω⁡(s,a)​(1−p⁡(s~∣s,a)​c​q​(x∣f⁡(x)))if ​i=2.p^{\mathrm{in}}_{x,\tilde{s},c,\omega}(i,s,a)\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}\omega(s,a)p(\tilde{s}\mid s,a)cq(x\mid f(x)),&\textnormal{if }i=1,\\ \omega(s,a)(1-p(\tilde{s}\mid s,a)cq(x\mid f(x)))&\textnormal{if }i=2.\\ \end{cases} (14)

3 Regret lower bound

This section proves Theorem 1.3. Section 3.1 outlines the proof, and Section 3.2 contains the details.

3.1 Proof outline

To prove Theorem 1.3, we construct a hard–to–learn subclass Λ∗\Lambda^{*} consisting of η\eta-regular and ℐη\mathcal{I}_{\eta}-identifiable BMDPs. We then lower bound the maximum regret over BMDPs in Λ∗\Lambda^{*}.

The proof takes inspiration from [24, Theorem 5]. It is, however, modified to (i) comply with Definitions 1.1 and 1.2 and (ii) obtain a worst-case regret lower bound. We distinguish three parts:

  1. Part 1.

    We define Λ∗\Lambda^{*} and show that all BMDPs in Λ∗\Lambda^{*} are η\eta-regular and ℐη\mathcal{I}_{\eta}-identifiable.

    Intuitively, Λ∗\Lambda^{*} is constructed so that rewards are received only upon visiting a specific subset of latent states, 𝒮1={⌊S/2⌋+1,…,S}\mathcal{S}_{1}=\{\lfloor S/2\rfloor+1,\ldots,S\}, say. In each latent state ss, there is one action as∗a_{s}^{*} that is ε\varepsilon more likely to transition to 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} relative to the other actions. Even if a context xx is revealed to belong to ss, the agent must still identify the optimal action as∗a_{s}^{*}. Conversely, even if as∗a_{s}^{*} is known for each ss, the agent must still infer which latent state xx corresponds to. By allowing ε\varepsilon to depend on whether ss belongs to 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} or 𝒮1c\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\mathrm{c}}, and tuning its value separately for each, we control which of these two learning challenges dominates. This gives rise to the two terms Ω⁡(A​TK)\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}) and Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) in (2).

  2. Part 2.

    The Ω⁡(A​TK)\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}) term in (2) arises from having to learn the transition probabilities even if the latent structure is revealed.

    To establish this, we analyze the induced MDP on the latent states. Following [11, 16], we use a change–of–measure argument to first lower bound the number of times an algorithm selects suboptimal actions while visiting 𝒮1c\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\mathrm{c}}. We then use the transition structure of the BMDPs in Λ∗\Lambda^{*} to bound how often 𝒮1c\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\mathrm{c}} is visited. Specifying ε=Θ⁡(A/TK)\varepsilon=\Theta(\sqrt{A/T_{K}}) yields the Ω⁡(A​TK)\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}) contribution in (2).

  3. Part 3.

    The Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) term in (2) arises from having to learn the latent structure even if the optimal actions are revealed.

    To formalize this, we fix a set of optimal actions {as∗}s\{a_{s}^{*}\}_{s} and consider the basic estimator that assign contexts xx to latent states ss whose action as∗a_{s}^{*} are chosen most. We then show that in BMDPs where {as∗}s\{a_{s}^{*}\}_{s} are indeed optimal, the regret is bounded from below by the number of contexts misclassified by this estimator. Applying Proposition 3.13, which lower bounds the maximum number of misclassifications over BMDPs in Λ∗\Lambda^{*} of any latent-state estimator, yields the Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) contribution when specifying ε=Θ⁡(1)\varepsilon=\Theta(1).

3.2 Proof of Theorem 1.3

Presume throughout this section that SS, AA, and HH satisfy (1).

Let 𝒮1={S/2+1,…,S}\mathcal{S}_{1}=\{S/2+1,\ldots,S\} and 𝒮0=𝒮1c\mathcal{S}_{0}=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\mathrm{c}}, and define ι:[S]→{0,1}\iota:[S]\rightarrow\{0,1\} as the map that assigns

s↦ι⁡(s):=arg⁡{i∈{0,1}:s∈𝒮i}.s\mapsto\iota(s)\vcentcolon=\arg\{i\in\{0,1\}:s\in\mathcal{S}_{i}\}. (16)

be a BMDP with:

  1. (i)

    latent state transition probabilities

  2. (ii)

    uniform emission probabilities: for s∈[S]s\in[S] and y∈f−1​(s)y\in f^{-1}(s), q⁡(y∣s)=1/|f−1​(s)|q(y\mid s)=1/|f^{-1}(s)|;

Figure 2 depicts the transition graph of such BMDPs schematically. Note that for every state ss, the specific action as∗a_{s}^{*} results in the highest chance to transition to 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. Because the only rewarding states are in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, this makes as∗a_{s}^{*} the unique optimal action for latent state ss. Ultimately, it is this structure that allows us to lower bound the regret (see Lemma 3.6).

To prove (2), we will consider hard–to–learn BMDPs that differ in both their optimal actions and decoding functions. This variation prevents algorithms from achieving low regret by tailoring its strategy to any single instance. We next define specific sets of optimal action assignments and decoding functions that capture the necessary structural diversity.

We consider decoding functions for which all latent states contain roughly the same number of contexts. The following lemma ensures a decomposition with the right properties is possible. Its proof is based on the paragraphs surrounding [47, (5.2)] and is given in Section C.2.

Lemma 3.2.

Let n0=⌊n/2⌋n_{0}=\lfloor n/2\rfloor and n1=n−n0n_{1}=n-n_{0}. Λ∗​(ε):=Λ⁡(ε,p~∗).\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon)\vcentcolon=\Lambda(\varepsilon,\tilde{p}^{*}). (22)

To prove Theorem 1.3, it suffices to establish (2) for some Φ∈Λ∗​(ε)\Phi\in\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon) for appropriate values of ε\varepsilon. We next provide a regret decomposition for BMDPs in Λ∗​(ε)\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon) that will allow us to do so.

The transition probabilities in (18) are chosen such that failing to select action as∗a_{s}^{*} when in latent state ss leads to an ει⁡(s)\varepsilon_{\iota(s)}-reduced probability of transitioning to 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, where it is possible to obtain a reward. Exploiting this, Section C.4 proves the following:

Lemma 3.6.

Write sk,h=f⁡(xk,h)s_{k,h}=f(x_{k,h}) and let Φ∈Λ∗​(ε)\Phi\in\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon). If ε0≤ε1\varepsilon_{0}\leq\varepsilon_{1}, then

RegK​(ℒ,Φ)≥∑i∈{0,1}RegK,i​(ℒ,Φ),\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)\geq\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}}\textnormal{Reg}_{K,i}(\mathcal{L};\Phi), (23)

where for i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\},

RegK,i(ℒ;Φ):=εi∑s∈𝒮i∑k=1K∑h=1H−1(𝔼Φ,ℒ[𝟙{sk,h=s}]−𝔼Φ,ℒ[𝟙{sk,h=s,ak,h=as∗}]).\textnormal{Reg}_{K,i}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)\vcentcolon=\varepsilon_{i}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{h=1}^{H-1}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}\bigl[\mathbbm{1}\{s_{k,h}=s\}\bigr]-\mathbb{E}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}\bigl[\mathbbm{1}\{s_{k,h}=s,a_{k,h}=a_{s}^{*}\}\bigr]\Bigr). Because 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℱ\mathcal{F} are countable and finite, so too is Λ∗​(ε)\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon). The arithmetic mean regret over Λ∗​(ε)\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon) therefore lower bounds the maximum regret. With Lemma 3.6, this implies that for ε0≤ε1\varepsilon_{0}\leq\varepsilon_{1},

supΦ∈Λ∗​(ε)RegK​(ℒ,Φ)≥∑i∈{0,1}RiwithRi:=1|Λ∗​(ε)|​∑Φ∈Λ∗​(ε)RegK,i​(ℒ,Φ).\sup_{\Phi\in\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon)}\textnormal{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)\geq\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}}R_{i}\quad\mathrm{with}\quad R_{i}\vcentcolon=\frac{1}{|\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon)|}\sum_{\Phi\in\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon)}\textnormal{Reg}_{K,i}(\mathcal{L};\Phi). (25)

We conclude Theorem 1.3’s proof by showing that there exist 0<ε0≤ε1<ϵ0<\varepsilon_{0}\leq\varepsilon_{1}<\epsilon such that R0=Ω⁡(A​TK)R_{0}=\Omega(\sqrt{AT_{K}}) and R1=Ω⁡(n)R_{1}=\Omega(n) whenever TK=Ω⁡(n∨A)T_{K}=\Omega(n\vee A). This is done next in Parts 2 and 3, respectively.

Part 2: Bounding the regret associated with learning the transition kernel

To bound R0R_{0} from below, we first upper bound the expected number of times the optimal action as∗a_{s}^{*} is played in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}. Lemma 3.7 relates the behavior of any algorithm on BMDPs Φ∈Λ∗​(ε)\Phi\in\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon) to its behavior on BMDPs Φ(0)\Phi^{(0)} for which all actions have the same probability of transitioning to 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. It is proven in Section C.5, and relies on a change–of–measure argument adapted from [36].

Lemma 3.7.

Let Φ∈Λ∗​(ε)\Phi\in\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon) have optimal actions {as∗}s∈𝒜\{a_{s}^{*}\}_{s}\in\mathcal{A}. Let Φ(0)\Phi^{(0)} be the BMDP obtained from Φ\Phi by setting ε0\varepsilon_{0} to zero. If ε0≤1/8\varepsilon_{0}\leq 1/8, then

Part 3: Bounding the regret associated with learning the latent structure

We first relate R1R_{1} to the number of misclassified contexts of an estimator based on ℒ\mathcal{L}’s selected actions.

Fix a set of optimal actions a∗∈𝒜a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}, and let πk=ℒk​(𝒟k,r)\pi_{k}=\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{k},r) denote the policy selected by a learning algorithm ℒ\mathcal{L} in episode kk. Define an estimate decoding function f^πk\hat{f}_{\pi_{k}} as follows:

For x∈f−1​(𝒮1)x\in f^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{1}), (29) assigns xx to the latent state whose optimal action is selected most frequently by πk\pi_{k}. Because our analysis only depends on f^πk|x∈f−1​(𝒮1)\hat{f}_{\pi_{k}}|_{x\in f^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{1})}, we arbitrarily set f^πk\hat{f}_{\pi_{k}} to 11 on x∈f−1​(𝒮0)x\in f^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{0}).

Recall from Definition 3.3 that each s∈𝒮1s\in\mathcal{S}_{1} has a distinct as∗a_{s}^{*}. Consequently, if f^πk\hat{f}_{\pi_{k}} misclassifies a context xx, then πk\pi_{k} selects af⁡(x)∗a_{f(x)}^{*} no more than half of the time by construction. Section C.8 uses this observation to bound RegK,1​(ℒ,Φ)\textnormal{Reg}_{K,1}(\mathcal{L};\Phi) in (23) by the expected number of misclassifications:

Lemma 3.10.

Let κ\kappa be as in (21) and p~∗\tilde{p}^{*} be given by Proposition 3.4. Fix a∗∈𝒜a^{*}\in\mathcal{A} and let f^πk\hat{f}_{\pi_{k}} be as in (29). Then, for f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} and Φ=Φ⁡(ε,p~∗,f,a∗)\Phi=\Phi(\varepsilon,\tilde{p}^{*},f,a^{*}),

RegK,1​(ℒ,Φ)≥ε1​(1−κ)​(H−1)2​(n+S+2)​∑k=1K𝔼Φ,ℒ​[|ℰ⁡(f^πk,f,𝒮1)|].\textnormal{Reg}_{K,1}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)\geq\frac{\varepsilon_{1}(1-\kappa)(H-1)}{2(n+S+2)}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}[|\mathcal{E}(\hat{f}_{\pi_{k}};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})|]. (30)

To bound R1R_{1} in (25) using Lemma 3.10, we will bound the expected number of misclassifications any estimate decoding function must make, averaged over the BMDPs in the hard–to–learn class. This is the content of Proposition 3.13 below, proven in the remainder of this section.

Recall 𝒞\mathcal{C}’s definition in Section 2.5. Let f^𝒞,k:=𝒞k​(𝒟k,r)\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}\vcentcolon=\mathcal{C}_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{k},r) denote the output of 𝒞\mathcal{C} after k−1k-1 episodes. Following [24, 35], we start by considering pairs of BMDPs that differ only at a single context xx. We then show that the probability of misclassifying xx cannot be small in both BMDPs under the same algorithm 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This is done in Section C.9, where we use a change–of–measure argument [36]. Specifically, we relate the misclassification probabilities in the two BMDPs to the expected log-likelihood ratio of the observed sequence of contexts. |ℱx|/|ℱ|≥1/18|\mathcal{F}_{x}|/|\mathcal{F}|\geq 1/18. Moreover, the map 𝒫x\mathcal{P}_{x}, restricted to ℱx\mathcal{F}_{x}, is a permutation of ℱx\mathcal{F}_{x} satisfying 𝒫x​f≠f\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq f for all f∈ℱxf\in\mathcal{F}_{x}.

4 Algorithm description

In this section we present a two–phase algorithm for the learning problem outlined in the Section 2.

Recall (9). For k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, a∈[A]a\in[A], and 𝒳1,𝒳2⊆[n]\mathcal{X}_{1},\mathcal{X}_{2}\subseteq[n], define the count

N^k​(𝒳1,a,𝒳2):=∑l=1k−1∑h=1H𝟙​{xl,h∈𝒳1,al,h=a,xl,h+1∈𝒳2},\hat{N}_{k}(\mathcal{X}_{1},a,\mathcal{X}_{2})\vcentcolon=\sum_{l=1}^{k-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbbm{1}\{x_{l,h}\in\mathcal{X}_{1},a_{l,h}=a,x_{l,h+1}\in\mathcal{X}_{2}\}, (39)

of the number of transitions from 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} to 𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{2} while choosing action aa prior to episode kk. Define also

N^k​(𝒳1,a):=N^k​(𝒳1,a,[n])andN^kto​(𝒳2):=∑aN^k​([n],a,𝒳2).\hat{N}_{k}(\mathcal{X}_{1},a)\vcentcolon=\hat{N}_{k}(\mathcal{X}_{1},a,[n])\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\hat{N}_{k}^{\mathrm{to}}(\mathcal{X}_{2})\vcentcolon=\sum_{a}\hat{N}_{k}([n],a,\mathcal{X}_{2}). (40)

These count the number of times aa was chosen while observing 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}, and the number of transitions to 𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{2} under any action, respectively.

Algorithms 1, 3 and 2 contain the basic components of the algorithm, which we discuss next.

4.1 Outer loop

Algorithm 1 describes the outer loop of the algorithm.

Phase 1 always selects the uniform policy. It lasts until at most Θclust\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}} transitions have been observed. These observations are used to estimate the decoding function with the UpdateLatentStates subroutine in Algorithm 2. Phase 2 selects the optimal policy for the Q-function computed by the ComputeQValues subroutine in Algorithm 3.

4.2 Latent state estimation

Algorithm 2 describes the UpdateLatentStates routine that Algorithm 1 uses to estimate the decoding function. It consists of two steps. First, an initial estimate is obtained using a spectral method. This is subsequently refined in an iterative improvement step. These steps correspond to [24, Algorithm 1] and [24, Algorithm 2], respectively. Appendix A reproduces their pseudocode in our notation.

4.3 Q-values routine

Algorithm 3 computes upper confidence bounds Q¯πk\bar{Q}^{\pi_{k}} on the optimal Q-function Qπ∗Q^{\pi^{*}}, defined in (6). It uses an estimate transition kernel to estimate Qπ∗Q^{\pi^{*}} with the Bellman-type recursion (7) initialized from QHπ∗​(x,a)=rH​(x,a)Q^{\pi^{*}}_{H}(x,a)=r_{H}(x,a). An exploration bonus is added to the reward rhr_{h} at each step to compensate for uncertainty about the expected next–state value. This ensures that the resulting Q-value estimate is indeed an upper confidence bound. The difference with [6] is that we use modified transition kernel estimates and exploration bonuses that exploit the structure of BMDPs.

Regarding the transition kernel, we first compute maximum likelihood estimators for the latent state transition kernel and emission probabilities on the learned latent states. These are given by

p^k​(s′∣s,a):=N^k​((f^alg)−1​(s),a,(f^alg)−1​(s′))1∨N^k​((f^alg)−1​(s),a),andq^k​(y∣s):=𝟙{y∈(f^alg)−1(s)}N^tok(y)1∨N^kto​((f^alg)−1​(s)),\hat{p}_{k}(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\vcentcolon=\frac{\hat{N}_{k}((\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s),a,(\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s^{\prime}))}{1\vee\hat{N}_{k}((\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s),a)},\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\hat{q}_{k}(y\mid s)\vcentcolon=\frac{\mathbbm{1}\{y\in(\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s)\}\hat{N}^{\mathrm{to}}_{k}(y)}{1\vee\hat{N}^{\mathrm{to}}_{k}((\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s))}, (41)

corresponding to the fraction of visits to (s,a)(s,a) that transition to s′s^{\prime} and the fraction of transitions to ss for which yy is observed, respectively. The BMDP transition kernel is then estimated by

P^k​(y∣x,a):=p^k​(f^alg​(y)∣f^alg​(x),a)​q^k​(y∣f^alg​(y)).\hat{P}_{k}(y\mid x,a)\vcentcolon=\hat{p}_{k}(\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}}(y)\mid\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}}(x),a)\hat{q}_{k}(y\mid\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}}(y)). (42)

Regarding the exploration bonuses, we define these as follows:

b^k​(s,a):=H2​ln⁡(2​H​S​A​Tk2)1∨N^k​((f^alg)−1​(s),a)+∑s′p^k​(s′∣s,a)​H2​ln⁡(2​H​S​Tk2)1∨N^kto​((f^alg)−1​(s′)).\hat{b}_{k}(s,a)\vcentcolon=\sqrt{\frac{H^{2}\ln(2HSAT_{k}^{2})}{1\vee\hat{N}_{k}((\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s),a)}}+\sum_{s^{\prime}}\hat{p}_{k}(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\sqrt{\frac{H^{2}\ln(2HST_{k}^{2})}{1\vee\hat{N}_{k}^{\mathrm{to}}((\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}})^{-1}(s^{\prime}))}}. (43)

Compared to [6], the bonuses b^k\hat{b}_{k} depend on the visitation counts of estimated latent states rather than individual contexts. They therefore decrease more quickly over time, leading to less exploration and lower regret. We will show that the estimated value function V¯h+1πk\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h+1} nonetheless is an upper confidence bound for the optimal value function Vh+1π∗V^{\pi^{*}}_{h+1}. This is possible because data aggregation within latent states reduces the variance of the estimate transition kernel used to compute V¯h+1πk\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h+1}.

Note, however, that this relies on the latent structure being inferred correctly by Algorithm 2. In general, uncertainty about this structure cannot fully be captured by bonuses assigned to latent state–action pairs [42]. Instead, we focus on the class of η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable BMDPs for which the latent structure can be learned efficiently through random exploration. This ensures the exploration time required for latent state estimation is bounded, enabling our two–phase approach.

5 Regret analysis of Algorithm 1

This section proves Theorem 1.4. Section 5.1 outlines the proof and Section 5.2 contains the details.

Throughout this section, we fix Φ\Phi and write ℙ=ℙΦ,ℒ\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}} and 𝔼=𝔼Φ,ℒ\mathbb{E}=\mathbb{E}_{\Phi,\mathcal{L}} with ℒ\mathcal{L} given by Algorithm 1.

5.1 Proof outline

The regret analysis here follows a strategy similar to those of other optimism-based algorithms [37, 39, 33, 6]. It, however, features modifications to exploit the latent structure of the BMDP.

The proof starts by decomposing the regret in (10) into different terms. These terms are then bounded separately. The regret bound in (3) is an aggregate of these bounds. Most of the proof is devoted to bounding the regret during this portion, which consists of three parts:

  1. Part 1.

    We define a sequence of events Ωk\Omega_{k} on which the estimate transition kernel P^k\hat{P}_{k} from (42) is close to the true kernel PP. Notably, Ωk\Omega_{k} is chosen such that the estimated decoding function f^alg\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}} equals its true value ff on Ωk\Omega_{k}.

    We also bound the probability that an Ωk\Omega_{k} fails. In particular, by refining proofs of [24], we show that for any c>0c>0, ℙ[f^alg≠f]=O(1/nc)\mathbb{P}[\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}}\neq f]=O(1/n^{c}) if Algorithm 1 explores sufficiently. This gives the O~​(TK/nc)\tilde{O}(T_{K}/n^{c}) term in (3).

    Note that Part 1 is the only place we use Definitions 1.1 and 1.2.

In Parts 2 and 3 next we consider the regret when ∩k∈[K]Ωk\cap_{k\in[K]}\Omega_{k} is true.

  1. Part 2.

    We show that on Ωk\Omega_{k}, V¯hπk​(x)\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h}(x) in Algorithm 3 is an upper confidence bound for the optimal value Vhπ∗​(x)V^{\pi^{*}}_{h}(x), i.e., that on Ωk\Omega_{k}, Vhπ∗​(x)≤V¯hπk​(x)V^{\pi^{*}}_{h}(x)\leq\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h}(x) for all h∈[H]h\in[H] and x∈[n]x\in[n].

    This implies that the regret per episode is bounded on Ωk\Omega_{k} by V¯1πk​(xk,1)−V1πk​(xk,1)\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1})-V^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1}).

  2. Part 3.

    We decompose V¯1πk​(xk,1)−V1πk​(xk,1)\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1})-V^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1}) into three terms. Of these, the most challenging is

    ∑h=1H−1𝔼[∑y(P^k(y∣xk,h,ak,h)−P(y∣xk,h,ak,h))(V¯h+1πk(y)−Vh+1π∗(y))∣𝒟k,xk,1].\sum_{h=1}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{y}(\hat{P}_{k}(y\mid x_{k,h},a_{k,h})-P(y\mid x_{k,h},a_{k,h}))(\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h+1}(y)-V^{\pi^{*}}_{h+1}(y))\mid\mathcal{D}_{k},x_{k,1}\biggr]. (44)

    This is due to the dependence between P^k\hat{P}_{k} and V¯h+1πk\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h+1}. Following [6], we relate this term to the exploration bonus b^k\hat{b}_{k}. The resulting corrections contribute the O~​(n​S​H3)\tilde{O}(nSH^{3}) term to (3).

    Afterwards, the remaining sum of exploration bonuses is bounded using a pigeonhole principle argument. Because the bonuses are independent of nn and depend only on the latent state of xk,hx_{k,h}, this yields the nn-independent O~​(H​S​A​TK)\tilde{O}(H\sqrt{SAT_{K}}) term in (3).

5.2 Proof of Theorem 1.4

Algorithm 1 accumulates regret in two phases. We bound the regret separately for each phase.

The first phase includes all episodes k∈[K]k\in[K] for which Tk=k​H≤ΘclustT_{k}=kH\leq\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}. Note that, for any given episode, V1π∗​(xk,1)−V1πk​(xk,1)≤HV^{\pi^{*}}_{1}(x_{k,1})-V_{1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,1})\leq H because the rewards are in [0,1][0,1]. It follows that the expected regret during the first phase is bounded by Θclust\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}, by construction of Algorithm 1.

The second phase is treated through decomposition as follows:

RegK​(ℒ,Φ)≤\displaystyle\text{Reg}_{K}(\mathcal{L};\Phi)\leq\, Θclust+H∑k∈[K]:Tk>Θclustℙ[(Ωk)c]+∑k∈[K]:Tk>Θclust𝔼[(V1π∗(xk,1)−V¯1πk(xk,1))𝟙{Ωk}]\displaystyle\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}+H\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in[K]:\\ T_{k}>\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{P}[(\Omega_{k})^{\mathrm{c}}]+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in[K]:\\ T_{k}>\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl(V^{\pi^{*}}_{1}(x_{k,1})-\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1})\bigr)\mathbbm{1}\{\Omega_{k}\}\bigr]
+∑k∈[K]:Tk>Θclust𝔼[(V¯1πk(xk,1)−V1πk(xk,1))𝟙{Ωk}]\displaystyle+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in[K]:\\ T_{k}>\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl(\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1})-V_{1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,1})\bigr)\mathbbm{1}\{\Omega_{k}\}\bigr]
=⁣:\displaystyle=\vcentcolon\, Θclust+R1+R2+R3.\displaystyle\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}+R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}. (45)

For k∈[K]k\in[K], we will consider

Next, we bound R1R_{1}, R2R_{2}, and R3R_{3} in (45). This corresponds to Parts 1, 2, and 3 from Section 5.1, respectively.

Part 1: Bounding the failure probability

We begin by bounding ℙ⁡[Ωf]\mathbb{P}[\Omega^{f}] by refining [24]’s analysis.

The first step is to address the gap between our notion of ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiability and the corresponding condition in [24]. As explained in Section B.2.2, [24] requires an asymptotic bound on limζ→∞minx⁡Iζ​(x,Φ)\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow\infty}\min_{x}I_{\zeta}(x;\Phi), rather than Iη​(x,Φ)I_{\eta}(x;\Phi). In Section D.1, we show that for η\eta-reachable BMDPs, these two conditions are equivalent:

Lemma 5.1.

Assume that Φ\Phi is η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable. Then there exists a constant ℐ′>0\mathcal{I}^{\prime}>0 that is independent of nn such that for all sufficiently large nn, limζ→∞minx⁡Iζ​(x,Φ)≥ℐ′\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow\infty}\min_{x}I_{\zeta}(x;\Phi)\geq\mathcal{I}^{\prime}.

Using Lemma 5.1, we can deduce the following corollary of [24, Theorem 3]:

Corollary 5.2.

If SS, AA and pp are independent of nn, μ=Unif⁡([n])\mu=\mathrm{Unif}([n]), and Φ\Phi is η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable, then there exist constants C,ℐ′>0C,\mathcal{I}^{\prime}>0 independent of nn such that: if Θclust=ω⁡(n)\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}=\omega(n), then Algorithm 2 misclassifies at most O⁡(n​exp⁡(−C⁡(Θclust/n)​ℐ′))O(n\exp(-C(\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}/n)\mathcal{I}^{\prime})) contexts with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1).

Consequently, under these assumptions, ℙ⁡[Ωf]=1−o⁡(1)\mathbb{P}[\Omega^{f}]=1-o(1) if Θclust=ω⁡(n​ln⁡n)\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}=\omega(n\ln n).

This result is, however, not enough for our purposes. We therefore refine it in three ways in Section D.2. First, we make the 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1) probability bound explicit by inspecting the proofs in [24] and keeping track of which events imply Ωf\Omega^{f}. Second, we sharpen the resulting probability bound from 1−O⁡(1/n)1-O(1/n) by showing that it can be 1−O⁡(1/nc)1-O(1/n^{c}) for any c>0c>0. Third, we allow SS, AA, and pp to depend on nn and account for this in the asymptotics. This gives the following result:

Proposition 5.3.

Assume Φ\Phi is η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable, and that Θclust=ω⁡(n​A​(S3∨ln⁡n))\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}=\omega(nA(S^{3}\vee\ln n)), μ=Unif⁡([n])\mu=\mathrm{Unif}([n]), A=nO⁡(1)A=n^{O(1)}, and H=O⁡(n)H=O(n). Then, for any c>0c>0, ℙ⁡[Ωf]=1−O⁡(1/nc)\mathbb{P}[\Omega^{f}]=1-O(1/n^{c}).

Given Ωf\Omega^{f}, it is straightforward to show that Ωk1,…,Ωk4\Omega_{k}^{1},\ldots,\Omega_{k}^{4} hold with probability 1−O⁡(1/Tk)1-O(1/T_{k}) using Hoeffding and Bernstein’s inequalities. Together with Proposition 5.3, this allows us to prove the following bound on R1R_{1} in :

Proposition 5.4.

Adopt the assumptions of Proposition 5.3, and let k∈[K]k\in[K] be such that Tk=k​H>ΘclustT_{k}=kH>\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}. Then, for any c>0c>0,

R1=H∑k∈[K]:Tk>Θclustℙ[(Ωk)c]=O(lnK+TKnc)=O~(1+TKnc).R_{1}=H\sum_{k\in[K]:T_{k}>\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}}\mathbb{P}[(\Omega_{k})^{\mathrm{c}}]=O\biggl(\ln K+\frac{T_{K}}{n^{c}}\biggr)=\tilde{O}\biggl(1+\frac{T_{K}}{n^{c}}\biggr). (47)

We next show that R2≤0R_{2}\leq 0 by proving that on Ωk\Omega_{k}, V¯hπk​(x)−Vhπ∗​(x)≥0\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h}(x)-V^{\pi^{*}}_{h}(x)\geq 0 for all hh and xx.

V¯hπk​(x)−Vhπ∗​(x)≥∑h′=hH−1𝔼Φ¯k,π∗[b^k(f^alg(xh′),ah′)+⟨P^k(⋅∣xh′,ah′)−P(⋅∣xh′,ah′),Vπ∗h′+1⟩∣xh=x].\begin{split}&\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{h}(x)-V^{\pi^{*}}_{h}(x)\\ &\geq\sum_{h^{\prime}=h}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\Phi}_{k},\pi^{*}}\bigl[\hat{b}_{k}(\hat{f}^{\textnormal{alg}}(x_{h^{\prime}}),a_{h^{\prime}})+\bigl\langle\hat{P}_{k}(\,\cdot\mid x_{h^{\prime}},a_{h^{\prime}})-P(\,\cdot\mid x_{h^{\prime}},a_{h^{\prime}}),V^{\pi^{*}}_{h^{\prime}+1}\bigr\rangle\mid x_{h}=x\bigr].\end{split} (48)

|⟨P^k(⋅∣x,a)−P(⋅∣x,a),Vh+1π∗⟩|≤b^k(f(x),a).|\langle\hat{P}_{k}(\,\cdot\mid x,a)-P(\,\cdot\mid x,a),V^{\pi^{*}}_{h+1}\rangle|\leq\hat{b}_{k}(f(x),a). (49)

contains the proof of Proposition 5.8. It is similar to that of [6, Lemma 3], which bounds Fk,hF_{k,h} for tabular MDPs. ≤∑h′=hH−1𝔼⁡[(B^k​(sk,h′,ak,h′,sk,h′+1)+1H​(2+1H)​(V¯h′+1πk​(xk,h′+1)−Vh′+1πk​(xk,h′+1)))​𝟙​{Ωk}],\displaystyle\leq\sum_{h^{\prime}=h}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}\biggl[\biggl(\hat{B}_{k}(s_{k,h^{\prime}},a_{k,h^{\prime}},s_{k,h^{\prime}+1})+\frac{1}{H}\biggl(2+\frac{1}{H}\biggr)\bigl(\bar{V}_{h^{\prime}+1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,h^{\prime}+1})-V_{h^{\prime}+1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,h^{\prime}+1})\bigr)\biggr)\mathbbm{1}\{\Omega_{k}\}\biggr],

Lemma 5.10’s assumptions are met for Bh=𝔼⁡[B^k​(sk,h,ak,h,sk,h+1)​𝟙​{Ωk}]B_{h}=\mathbb{E}[\hat{B}_{k}(s_{k,h},\allowbreak a_{k,h},\allowbreak s_{k,h+1})\mathbbm{1}\{\Omega_{k}\}] by Proposition 5.9 and because V¯Hπk​(x)=VHπk​(x)=maxa∈[A]⁡rH​(x,a)\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{H}(x)=V^{\pi_{k}}_{H}(x)=\max_{a\in[A]}r_{H}(x,a) by definition. Together with B^k≥0\hat{B}_{k}\geq 0, we conclude that

𝔼⁡[(V¯1πk​(xk,1)−V1πk​(xk,1))​𝟙​{Ωk}]≤e2​∑h=1H−1𝔼⁡[B^k​(sk,h,ak,h,sk,h+1)].\mathbb{E}[(\bar{V}_{1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,1})-V_{1}^{\pi_{k}}(x_{k,1}))\mathbbm{1}\{\Omega_{k}\}]\leq e^{2}\sum_{h=1}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}[\hat{B}_{k}(s_{k,h},a_{k,h},s_{k,h+1})]. (56)

Observe now that B^k​(s,a,s′)\hat{B}_{k}(s,a,s^{\prime}) depends inversely on the visitation count of the triple (s,a,s′)(s,a,s^{\prime}). Hence, once a triple is visited, its corresponding B^k​(s,a,s′)\hat{B}_{k}(s,a,s^{\prime}) dereases in subsequent episodes. Proposition 5.9 was formulated precisely so that we can exploit this fact. We do so in , where we prove our final bound on R3R_{3}. This result is better than its analogue for tabular MDPs because the visitation count of a latent state increases more quickly than that of a single context.

Proposition 5.11.

If TK=K​H=Ω⁡(H4​S3​A)T_{K}=KH=\Omega(H^{4}S^{3}A), then

R3=∑k∈[K]:Tk>Θclust𝔼[(V¯πk1(xk,1)−Vπk1(xk1))𝟙{Ωk}]=O~(HS​A​TK+nH3).\begin{split}R_{3}=\sum_{k\in[K]:T_{k}>\Theta^{\textnormal{clust}}}\mathbb{E}[(\bar{V}^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k,1})-V^{\pi_{k}}_{1}(x_{k_{1}}))\mathbbm{1}\{\Omega_{k}\}]=\tilde{O}(H\sqrt{SAT_{K}}+nH^{3}).\end{split} (57)

Finally — the proof of Theorem 1.4 is done by noting that the assumptions of Theorem 1.4 are the same as those of Propositions 5.4, 5.7 and 5.11, and using these to bound R1R_{1}, R2R_{2}, and R3R_{3} in (45).

6 Numerical proof of concept

We now demonstrate the method and briefly compare its performance to the UCBVI algorithms of [6], which do not exploit the latent structure.

We fix A=3A=3 and H=20H=20. For n∈{100,200}n\in\{100,200\} and S∈{3,6}S\in\{3,6\}, we sample p(⋅∣s,a)p(\,\cdot\mid s,a) independently from Dir​(1,…,1)\textnormal{Dir}(1,\ldots,1) for each ss and aa. Here, Dir​(α1,…,αk)\textnormal{Dir}(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) denotes the kk-dimensional Dirichlet distribution. Similarly, we sample {q⁡(y∣s)}y∈f−1​(s)\{q(y\mid s)\}_{y\in f^{-1}(s)} independently from Dir​(n,…,n)\textnormal{Dir}(\sqrt{n},\ldots,\sqrt{n}) for each ss. We set each latent state to have the same number of contexts. These BMDPs turned out to be η\eta-reachable and ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiable with η≈25.5\eta\approx 25.5 and ℐ≈0.12\mathcal{I}\approx 0.12 for S=3S=3, and η≈33.6\eta\approx 33.6 and ℐ≈0.49\mathcal{I}\approx 0.49 for S=6S=6. The rewards rh​(x,a)r_{h}(x,a) are sampled independently from Unif​([0,1])\textnormal{Unif}([0,1]) for each xx, aa, and hh.

Figure 3 shows the cumulative regret over K=105K=10^{5} episodes for UCBVI–CH, UCBVI–BF, and Algorithm 1. Here, we averaged over 10 runs for a fixed BMDP. Algorithm 1 eventually achieves lower regret for all parameter configurations in Figure 3. The difference increases for larger nn and smaller SS. Notably, Algorithm 1’s performance stays the same when nn is increased.

Appendix A Latent state estimation algorithm

We here briefly recall [24, Algorithm 1] and [24, Algorithm 2], which are used in Algorithm 2 to estimate the decoding function. We do so to relate their notation to ours, and for ease of reference during the proofs, specifically that of Proposition 5.3.

A.1 Spectral Clustering Algorithm

The first step of Algorithm 2 consists of the spectral algorithm [24, Algorithm 1], whose pseudocode we reproduce here in our notation.

The procedure starts by trimming the transition count matrices matrices 𝐍^a\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{a} for each aa by setting to zero each row and column corresponding to contexts in Γa\Gamma_{a}. Here, Γa⊂[n]\Gamma_{a}\subset[n] are the contexts that remain after removing the ⌊nexp(−Tk/(nA)ln(Tk/(nA)))⌋\lfloor n\exp(-T_{k}/(nA)\ln(T_{k}/(nA)))\rfloor contexts that are visited most often when choosing action aa.

Next, a rank-SS approximation 𝐑^a\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{a} of the resulting matrix 𝐍^Γ,a\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{\Gamma,a} is constructed by calculating the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) 𝐍^aΓ=𝐔a⊺​diag​(σa,1,…,σa,n)​𝐕a\hat{\mathbf{N}}^{\Gamma}_{a}=\mathbf{U}_{a}^{\intercal}\text{diag}(\sigma_{a,1},\ldots,\sigma_{a,n})\mathbf{V}_{a} where 𝐔a,𝐕a\mathbf{U}_{a},\mathbf{V}_{a} are two n×nn\times n orthonormal matrices, and σa,1≥σa,2≥…≥σa,n\sigma_{a,1}\geq\sigma_{a,2}\geq\ldots\geq\sigma_{a,n} are the singular values of 𝐍^aΓ\hat{\mathbf{N}}^{\Gamma}_{a} in decreasing order, and defining for each aa

𝐑^a:=𝐔a⊺​diag​(σa,1,…,σa,S,0,…,0)​𝐕a.\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{a}\vcentcolon=\mathbf{U}_{a}^{\intercal}\text{diag}(\sigma_{a,1},\ldots,\sigma_{a,S},0,\ldots,0)\mathbf{V}_{a}. (58)

The matrices 𝐑^a\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{a} are subsequently concatenated to obtain the “fat” matrix 𝐑^\hat{\mathbf{R}}. After normalizing each row of 𝐑^\hat{\mathbf{R}} by its corresponding ℓ1\ell^{1}-norm, a weighted KK-medians procedure is used to estimate f^0\hat{f}_{0}. We refer to [24, Eqn. (61)] for the exact optimization problem that is solved to determine f^0\hat{f}_{0}.

A.2 Iterative Improvement Algorithm

The second step of Algorithm 2 consists of the iterative improvement algorithm [24, Algorithm 2], whose pseudocode we reproduce here in our notation.

Starting from some initial estimate f^0\hat{f}_{0}, at each iteration ℓ=0,1,…\ell=0,1,\ldots it uses the current estimate decoding function f^ℓ\hat{f}_{\ell} to estimate the latent state transition probabilities from N^\hat{N}. Note that it also estimates the backward transition probabilities pbwd​(s,a∣s′)p^{\mathrm{bwd}}(s,a\mid s^{\prime}), i.e., the probability that action aa was taken in latent state ss given that we are currently in latent state s′s^{\prime}. These estimates are then used to estimate for each context xx, the log-likelihood of the observed data over each potential new assignment f^ℓ+1​(x)=s′\hat{f}_{\ell+1}(x)=s^{\prime}.

The context xx is assigned to the latent state s′s^{\prime} that maximizes this estimate log-likelihood. This greedy, local likelihood maximization is repeated ⌈ln⁡n⌉\lceil\ln n\rceil times, each time using the updated decoding to estimate a new log-likelihood function. In Algorithm 2, the improvement algorithm is initialized with the decoding function f^0\hat{f}_{0} returned by the spectral clustering algorithm.

Appendix B On the structural properties

This section further explains Definitions 1.2 and 1.1 and relates them to analogous properties used in the literature.

B.1 Explanation of the structural properties

B.1.1 Reachability

Definition 1.1 imposes a degree of regularity on the latent state transition probabilities, the emission probabilities, and the number of contexts per latent state. Concretely, since ∑s′p⁡(s′∣s,a)=∑y∈f−1​(s)q⁡(y∣s)=∑s|f−1​(s)|/n=1\sum_{s^{\prime}}p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)=\sum_{y\in f^{-1}(s)}q(y\mid s)=\sum_{s}|f^{-1}(s)|/n=1, Definition 1.1 implies that for sufficiently large nn,

1η​S≤p(s′∣s,a)≤ηS,1η​|f−1​(s)|≤q(y∣s)≤η|f−1​(s)|,andnη​S≤|f−1(s)|≤η​nS\frac{1}{\eta S}\leq p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\leq\frac{\eta}{S},\quad\frac{1}{\eta|f^{-1}(s)|}\leq q(y\mid s)\leq\frac{\eta}{|f^{-1}(s)|},\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\frac{n}{\eta S}\leq|f^{-1}(s)|\leq\frac{\eta n}{S} (59)

for s,s′∈[S]s,s^{\prime}\in[S], y∈f−1​(s)y\in f^{-1}(s). In turn, this implies that in expectation, and up to a constant factor, all contexts are observed equally often under any exploration policy.

B.1.2 Identifiability

Definition 1.2 imposes a minimum degree of separation between different latent states. In particular, it ensures this separation remains bounded away from zero as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.

Concretely, the quantity Is~​(x,c,Φ,π)I_{\tilde{s}}(x;c,\Phi,\pi) in (13) is the leading-order term in the expansion of the log-likelihood ratio of the context–action sequence between Φ\Phi and the confusing BMDP Ψ\Psi in [24, Appendix D] as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. The parameter c>0c>0 controls the emission probability of xx in s~\tilde{s}. Thus, by ensuring that minx⁡Iη​(x,Φ)\min_{x}I_{\eta}(x;\Phi) remains bounded away from zero, Definition 1.2 prevents two distinct latent states from having asymptotically indistinguishable transition and emission probabilities.

B.2 Relation to literature

Analogues of Definitions 1.1 and 1.2 are common in the BMDP literature. See, for example, [12, Definition 2.1 and/or Assumption 3.2] as well as [31, Definition 6].

Our formulation is based on [24], in order to leverage their results on latent state estimation. In turn, [24] builds on related conditions from the block model literature, including BMCs [35] and (labeled) SBMs [1, 45, 15].

B.2.1 Reachability

When SS is independent of nn, any η\eta-reachable BMDP satisfies [24, Assumptions 2 and 3]. Both η\eta-reachability and [24, Assumptions 2 and 3] are stronger than the reachability conditions typically considered in the BMDP literature. For example, [12, 31] require that every state is reachable under some policy, whereas η\eta-reachability enforces a uniform degree of reachability under any policy.

As highlighted in Section 1.5.1, this difference reflects distinct objectives. Works such as [12, 31] aim to design efficient exploration policies to learn the latent structure using function approximation. By contrast, our focus is on analyzing explicit recovery algorithms with provable guarantees in the line of [35, 24].

B.2.2 Identifiability

ℐ\mathcal{I}-identifiability is closely related to [24, Theorem 3]’s assumption I⁡(Φ)>0I(\Phi)>0, where

I⁡(Φ):=−nTk​ln⁡(12​η​S​n​∑xexp⁡(−Tkn​I​(x,Φ)))I(\Phi)\vcentcolon=-\frac{n}{T_{k}}\ln\biggl(\frac{1}{2\eta Sn}\sum_{x}\exp\biggl(-\frac{T_{k}}{n}I(x;\Phi)\biggr)\biggr) (60)

with

I⁡(x,Φ):=limζ→∞Iζ​(x,Φ)=min⁡infc>0s~≠f⁡(x)⁡Is~​(x,c,Φ,πU).I(x;\Phi)\vcentcolon=\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow\infty}I_{\zeta}(x;\Phi)=\min_{\tilde{s}\neq f(x)}\inf_{c>0}I_{\tilde{s}}(x;c,\Phi,\pi_{U}). (61)

When Tk=ω⁡(n)T_{k}=\omega(n) and SS, AA and pp are independent of nn, one can show that the conditions

I⁡(Φ)=Ω⁡(1)andminx⁡I⁡(x,Φ)=Ω⁡(1)I(\Phi)=\Omega(1)\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\min_{x}I(x;\Phi)=\Omega(1) (62)

are equivalent. In our framework, however, SS, AA, and pp do depend on nn. In this case, minx⁡I⁡(x,Φ)=Ω⁡(1)\min_{x}I(x;\Phi)=\Omega(1) still implies I⁡(Φ)=Ω⁡(1)I(\Phi)=\Omega(1), but the converse need not hold. Definition 1.2 therefore requires an analogue of the stronger condition minx⁡I⁡(x,Φ)=Ω⁡(1)\min_{x}I(x;\Phi)=\Omega(1).

Definition 1.2’s requirement, however, is slightly weaker than minx⁡I⁡(x,Φ)=Ω⁡(1)\min_{x}I(x;\Phi)=\Omega(1) because Iη​(x,Φ)≥I⁡(x,Φ)I_{\eta}(x;\Phi)\geq I(x;\Phi); (compare the infima in (15) and (61)). Section D.1 contains a proof that that Definition 1.2 nonetheless implies minx⁡I⁡(x,Φ)=Ω⁡(1)\min_{x}I(x;\Phi)=\Omega(1), ensuring compatibility with [24].

For further comparisons with other notions of identifiability in the BMDP literature, see [24, Appendix D.3.5].

Appendix C Proofs for Section 3

C.1 Bounds on visitation rates

The following lemma bounds visitation rates and is used throughout this section.

The proof of Lemma 3.2 adapts the argument given after [47, Eqn. (5.2)], modifying it slightly to avoid a case distinction between S/2=2S/2=2 and S/2≥3S/2\geq 3. We do not, however, pursue an upper bound or a bound on 𝔰i0\mathfrak{s}_{i}^{0}, both of which are derived in [47].

Fix i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}. Let ri:=ni−⌊2​ni/S⌋​S/2r_{i}\vcentcolon=n_{i}-\lfloor 2n_{i}/S\rfloor S/2 and note that 0≤ri≤S/2−10\leq r_{i}\leq S/2-1. We consider separately the cases ri≥S/36r_{i}\geq S/36 and ri<S/36r_{i}<S/36.

If instead ri<S/36r_{i}<S/36, let 𝔰i−1=⌊S/6⌋\mathfrak{s}^{-1}_{i}=\lfloor S/6\rfloor, 𝔰i0=S/2−2​⌊S/6⌋−ri\mathfrak{s}^{0}_{i}=S/2-2\lfloor S/6\rfloor-r_{i}, and 𝔰i+1=ri+⌊S/6⌋\mathfrak{s}^{+1}_{i}=r_{i}+\lfloor S/6\rfloor. Fix k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and an estimation algorithm 𝒞\mathcal{C}. As in Section C.5 we set up to apply [36, Lemma H.1], this time with ℳ≡Φ(2)\mathcal{M}\equiv\Phi^{(2)}, ℳ′≡Φ(1)\mathcal{M}^{\prime}\equiv\Phi^{(1)}, and Z≡𝟙{f^𝒞,k(x)=f(1)(x)}Z\equiv\mathbbm{1}\{\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}(x)=f^{(1)}(x)\}. ≥kl(ℙΦ(2),ℒ[f^𝒞,k(x)=f(1)(x)],ℙΦ(1),ℒ[f^𝒞,k(x)=f(1)(x)]).\displaystyle\geq\textnormal{kl}\bigl(\mathbb{P}_{\Phi^{(2)},\mathcal{L}}[\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}(x)=f^{(1)}(x)],\mathbb{P}_{\Phi^{(1)},\mathcal{L}}[\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}(x)=f^{(1)}(x)]\bigr).

We claim that there exists a constant C>0C>0 depending only on η\eta such that for all sufficiently large nn,

∑x∑aKL(P(2)(⋅∣x,a),P(1)(⋅∣x,a))∑k′=1k−1∑h=1H𝔼Φ(2),ℒ[𝟙{xk′,h=x,ak′,h=a}]≤CTkn.\displaystyle\sum_{x}\sum_{a}\textnormal{KL}(P^{(2)}(\,\cdot\mid x,a),P^{(1)}(\,\cdot\mid x,a))\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{k-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\Phi^{(2)},\mathcal{L}}[\mathbbm{1}\{x_{k^{\prime},h}=x,a_{k^{\prime},h}=a\}]\leq C\frac{T_{k}}{n}. (138)

The result (31) would then follow because combining (136)–(138) gives

(1−ℙΦ(2),ℒ[f^𝒞,k(x)≠f(2)(x)])ln1ℙΦ(1),ℒ[f^𝒞,k≠f(1)(x)]≤CTkn+ln2.(1-\mathbb{P}_{\Phi^{(2)},\mathcal{L}}[\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}(x)\neq f^{(2)}(x)])\ln\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\Phi^{(1)},\mathcal{L}}[\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}\neq f^{(1)}(x)]}\leq C\frac{T_{k}}{n}+\ln 2. (139)

Since ℙΦ(2),ℒ[f^𝒞,k(x)≠f(2)(x)]∈[0,1)\mathbb{P}_{\Phi^{(2)},\mathcal{L}}[\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}(x)\neq f^{(2)}(x)]\in[0,1) by assumption and exp(−ln2/(1−p))≥1/2\exp(-\ln 2/(1-p))\geq 1/2 for p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), this implies that

Proof that 𝒫x|ℱx\mathcal{P}_{x}|_{\mathcal{F}_{x}} is a permutation without fixed points. We next prove that 𝒫x|ℱx\mathcal{P}_{x}|_{\mathcal{F}_{x}} is a permutation of ℱx\mathcal{F}_{x} for which 𝒫x​f≠f\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq f for all f∈ℱxf\in\mathcal{F}_{x}. Given the identifications above, the map f|x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]↦𝒫x​f|x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]f|_{x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]}\mapsto\mathcal{P}_{x}f|_{x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]} can be identified with the map σ0↦σ⁡[σ0]\sigma_{0}\mapsto\sigma[\sigma_{0}] from [47, Section 6.2]. There, it is asserted but not explicitly proven that this map is a permutation without fixed points. For completeness, we include a proof of this fact here.

Given some nonempty subset 𝒱⊂ℕ+\mathcal{V}\subset\mathbb{N}_{+} and an element v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, let 𝒱v+:={v′∈𝒱:v′>v}\mathcal{V}_{v}^{+}\vcentcolon=\{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}:v^{\prime}>v\} denote the set of elements larger than vv. Then define the map

In other words, 𝒯𝒱​(v)\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}}(v) selects the next largest element of 𝒱\mathcal{V} if it exists, and otherwise returns the smallest element of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. It is clear that 𝒯𝒱​(v)≠v\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}}(v)\neq v unless 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a singleton, and that the map 𝒯𝒱\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}} is injective.

The map 𝒫x\mathcal{P}_{x} in (34) can now be expressed as:

Next fix x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor] and f∈ℱxf\in\mathcal{F}_{x}. We first verify that 𝒫x​f∈ℱx\mathcal{P}_{x}f\in\mathcal{F}_{x} and 𝒫x​f≠f\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq f.

  1. (i)

    𝒫x​f≠f\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq f holds because 𝒮10​(f)\mathcal{S}_{1}^{0}(f) is nonempty by Lemma 3.2, and therefore (157) and the properties of 𝒯\mathcal{T} imply that 𝒫x​f​(x)≠f⁡(x)\mathcal{P}_{x}f(x)\neq f(x), and hence 𝒫x​f≠f\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq f.

  2. (ii)

    3.3(i) holds because by the previous point xx gets moved to a latent state in 𝒮10​(f)\mathcal{S}_{1}^{0}(f) and is therefore still in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} under 𝒫x​f\mathcal{P}_{x}f; hence, (𝒫x​f)−1​(𝒮1)={⌊n/2⌋+1,…,n}(\mathcal{P}_{x}f)^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{1})=\{\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1,\ldots,n\} as required.

  3. (iii)

    3.3(ii) and 3.3(iii) hold because after moving xx from f⁡(x)f(x) to 𝒫x​f​(x)\mathcal{P}_{x}f(x), the former latent state contains one fewer context while the latter contains one more. Since f⁡(x)∈𝒮1+1​(f)f(x)\in\mathcal{S}_{1}^{+1}(f) and 𝒫x​f​(x)∈𝒮10​(f)\mathcal{P}_{x}f(x)\in\mathcal{S}_{1}^{0}(f), and because f⁡(y)=𝒫x​f​(y)f(y)=\mathcal{P}_{x}f(y) for y≠xy\neq x, the resulting sets 𝒮iσ​(𝒫x​f)\mathcal{S}_{i}^{\sigma}(\mathcal{P}_{x}f) have the same cardinalities as 𝒮iσ​(f)\mathcal{S}_{i}^{\sigma}(f) for i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\} and σ∈{−1,0,+1}\sigma\in\{-1,0,+1\}.

  4. (iv)

    Finally, x∈𝒮1+1​(𝒫x​f)x\in\mathcal{S}_{1}^{+1}(\mathcal{P}_{x}f) follows immediately from point (iii).

Together, points (i)–(iv) prove that if f∈ℱxf\in\mathcal{F}_{x}, then 𝒫x​f∈ℱx\mathcal{P}_{x}f\in\mathcal{F}_{x} and 𝒫x​f≠f\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq f.

We conclude the proof by showing that 𝒫x\mathcal{P}_{x} restricted to ℱx\mathcal{F}_{x} is a permutation. Since ℱx\mathcal{F}_{x} is a finite set, it suffices to show that 𝒫x\mathcal{P}_{x} is injective on ℱx\mathcal{F}_{x}. Hence, let f,g∈ℱxf,g\in\mathcal{F}_{x} and assume that f≠gf\neq g. We show that 𝒫x​f≠𝒫x​g\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq\mathcal{P}_{x}g. Since 𝒫x​f​(y)=f⁡(y)\mathcal{P}_{x}f(y)=f(y) for y≠xy\neq x it immediately follows that 𝒫x​f≠𝒫x​g\mathcal{P}_{x}f\neq\mathcal{P}_{x}g whenever there exists y≠xy\neq x such that f⁡(y)≠g⁡(y)f(y)\neq g(y).

Assume therefore that no such yy exists, in which case f≠gf\neq g implies f⁡(x)≠g⁡(x)f(x)\neq g(x). It suffices to show that 𝒫x​f​(x)≠𝒫x​g​(x)\mathcal{P}_{x}f(x)\neq\mathcal{P}_{x}g(x). Since f⁡(x)∈𝒮1+1​(f)f(x)\in\mathcal{S}_{1}^{+1}(f) and g⁡(x)∈𝒮1+1​(g)g(x)\in\mathcal{S}_{1}^{+1}(g) by (35), f⁡(x)≠g⁡(x)f(x)\neq g(x), and f⁡(y)=g⁡(y)f(y)=g(y) for all y≠xy\neq x, it follows that 𝒮10​(f)∪{f⁡(x)}=𝒮10​(g)∪{g⁡(x)}=:𝒮¯\mathcal{S}^{0}_{1}(f)\cup\{f(x)\}=\mathcal{S}^{0}_{1}(g)\cup\{g(x)\}=\vcentcolon\bar{\mathcal{S}}. The result now follows from (157) and injectivity of the map 𝒯𝒮¯\mathcal{T}_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}}. ∎

C.11 Proof of Proposition 3.13

Take nn large enough for the implication of Lemma 3.11 to hold, and for mins⁡|f−1​(s)|≥1\min_{s}|f^{-1}(s)|\geq 1 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} to hold.

Fix a set of optimal actions a∗∈𝒜a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}, a learning algorithm ℒ\mathcal{L}, and parameters ε\varepsilon and p~∗\tilde{p}^{*} as in Definition 3.5, and adopt the notation in (32). Also fix a number of episodes k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, and recall that f^𝒞,k=𝒞k​(𝒟k,r)\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k}=\mathcal{C}_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{k},r) denotes the output of the estimation algorithm 𝒞\mathcal{C} after k−1k-1 episodes.

The proof follows the outline described above Proposition 3.13, but involves additional steps to account for the permutation γf∗\gamma^{*}_{f} appearing in (33) and (36). We first define an auxiliary quantity which we modify the decomposition in (33) with.

Recall (11). For any two decoding functions ff and f^\hat{f} and any 𝒮⊂[S]\mathcal{S}\subset[S], we define the set

Γ∗(f^;f,𝒮):=arg​minγ∈Perm⁡([S])|∪s∈𝒮f^−1(γ(s))∖f−1(s)|.\Gamma^{*}(\hat{f};f,\mathcal{S})\vcentcolon=\argmin_{\gamma\in\mathrm{Perm}([S])}\bigl|\cup_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\hat{f}^{-1}(\gamma(s))\setminus f^{-1}(s)\bigr|. (158)

Observe that the number of misclassifications of f^\hat{f} at 𝒮\mathcal{S} can be expressed as

|ℰ⁡(f^,f,𝒮)|=∑γ∈Γ∗​(f^,f,𝒮)∑x∈f−1​(𝒮)𝟙{γ−1∘f^(x)≠f(x)}|Γ∗​(f^,f,𝒮)|.|\mathcal{E}(\hat{f};f,\mathcal{S})|=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma^{*}(\hat{f},f;\mathcal{S})}\frac{\sum_{x\in f^{-1}(\mathcal{S})}\mathbbm{1}\{\gamma^{-1}\circ\hat{f}(x)\neq f(x)\}}{|\Gamma^{*}(\hat{f};f,\mathcal{S})|}. (159)

We also define the local misclassification rate at x∈f−1​(𝒮)x\in f^{-1}(\mathcal{S}) as

εx​(f^,f,𝒮):=∑γ∈Γ∗​(f^,f,𝒮)𝟙{γ−1∘f^(x)≠f(x)}|Γ∗​(f^,f,𝒮)|.\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f};f,\mathcal{S})\vcentcolon=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma^{*}(\hat{f},f;\mathcal{S})}\frac{\mathbbm{1}\{\gamma^{-1}\circ\hat{f}(x)\neq f(x)\}}{|\Gamma^{*}(\hat{f};f,\mathcal{S})|}. (160)

The expected number of misclassifications can now be decomposed in terms of the εx\varepsilon^{x} as follows. Note that because f−1​(𝒮1)={⌊n/2⌋+1,…,n}f^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{1})=\{\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1,\ldots,n\} for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, we have that

1|ℱ|​∑f∈ℱ𝔼f​[|ℰk​(f^𝒞,k,f,𝒮1)|]=∑x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]1|ℱ|​∑f∈ℱ𝔼f​[εx​(f^𝒞,k,f,𝒮1)].\begin{split}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\mathbb{E}_{f}[|\mathcal{E}_{k}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})|]=\sum_{x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\mathbb{E}_{f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})].\end{split} (161)

Then apply Lemma 3.12 to the right-hand side of (161) in a manner analogous to (36) to obtain

1|ℱ|​∑f∈ℱ𝔼f​[|ℰk​(f^𝒞,k,f,𝒮1)|]≥∑x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]136​|ℱx|​∑f∈ℱx(𝔼f​[εx​(f^𝒞,k,f,𝒮1)]+𝔼𝒫x​f​[εx​(f^𝒞,k,𝒫x​f,𝒮1)]).\begin{split}&\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\mathbb{E}_{f}[|\mathcal{E}_{k}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})|]\\ &\geq\sum_{x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]}\frac{1}{36|\mathcal{F}_{x}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{x}}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{x}f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};\mathcal{P}_{x}f,\mathcal{S}_{1})]\bigr).\end{split} (162)

To bound (162) for all estimation algorithms 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we take the infimum of both sides over all such 𝒞\mathcal{C} and use that the infimum of a sum is bounded by the sum of the infima:

≥∑x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]136​|ℱx|​∑f∈ℱxinf𝒞(𝔼f​[εx​(f^𝒞,k,f,𝒮1)]+𝔼𝒫x​f​[εx​(f^𝒞,k,𝒫x​f,𝒮1)]).\displaystyle\geq\sum_{x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]}\frac{1}{36|\mathcal{F}_{x}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{x}}\inf_{\mathcal{C}}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{x}f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C},k};\mathcal{P}_{x}f,\mathcal{S}_{1})]\bigr).

Now observe that because ff and 𝒫x​f\mathcal{P}_{x}f differ only at x∈[n]∖[⌊n/2⌋]x\in[n]\setminus[\lfloor n/2\rfloor], it must be that

≥inf𝒞(𝔼f​[εx​(f^𝒞x,k,f,𝒮1)]+𝔼𝒫x​f​[εx​(f^𝒞x,k,𝒫x​f,𝒮1)]).\displaystyle\geq\inf_{\mathcal{C}}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C}^{x},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1})]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{x}f}[\varepsilon^{x}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C}^{x},k};\mathcal{P}_{x}f,\mathcal{S}_{1})]\bigr). (165)

Note that for all sufficiently large nn, the set Γ∗​(f^𝒞x,k,f,𝒮1)\Gamma^{*}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{C}^{x},k};f,\mathcal{S}_{1}) only contains the identity permutation. where in passing to the last line we used that the infimum over 𝒞\mathcal{C} includes all algorithms of the form in (164).

We first prove (38).

(171)

R1≥ε1​(1−κ)​(H−1)288​11+S+2n​∑k=1Kexp⁡(−C​Tkn).R_{1}\geq\frac{\varepsilon_{1}(1-\kappa)(H-1)}{288}\frac{1}{1+\frac{S+2}{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\exp\biggl(-C\frac{T_{k}}{n}\biggr). (172)

Lemma D.1 follows as a corollary from the proof of [24, Proposition 12]. The quantity Ij∗​(x,c,Φ,πU)I^{*}_{j}(x;c,\Phi,\pi_{U}) for j∈[S]j\in[S] is also closely related to the quantity I~j​(x,c,Φ)\tilde{I}_{j}(x;c,\Phi) from [24, Eqn. (37)-(39)]. Notice firstly that the lower bound in [24, Lemma 6] is symmetric with respect to the arguments of the KL-divergence appearing therein.
